name: ai-privacy
context: An agent touches personal or otherwise privacy-sensitive data across several trust boundaries — the user's prompt, retrieved documents, tool-call arguments sent to third-party services, persistent memory, and the final response — and each crossing is a place where data that the downstream party does not need becomes disclosed. The failure is not a leak the system tries to prevent and fails at; it is that the agent optimises for task completion and therefore over-shares by construction. Measured over realistic tasks, agents routinely pack privacy-sensitive data into tool-call arguments beyond what the invoked tool requires, because the agent optimises completion, not privacy. Standard defences are insufficient on their own: call-level gating can only allow or block (it cannot rewrite arguments), token-level PII detectors are pattern matchers that miss implicit sensitivity (a hospital name implies a diagnosis; a temporal pattern reveals a routine) and are schema-unaware, and uniform redaction ignores the trust level of the destination. This pattern therefore applies data minimisation proactively rather than relying on detection: a middleware sits between the agent and every tool, classifies the privacy-sensitive content actually present in the arguments against the receiving tool's schema and trust level, computes a privacy cost, and rewrites the arguments to the minimum necessary data that still preserves task validity. It pairs that argument-level rewrite with minimisation over the other boundaries — redact before entering context, minimise before persisting to memory, omit before responding — and tracks flow against the user's actual disclosure expectations, because whether something is a leak depends on context, not just on the content.
benefits: Removes over-sharing at the source rather than catching it after disclosure, since minimization rewrites arguments to the minimum needed before the tool is ever called
Preserves task validity: argument-level rewriting trims only what the tool schema does not require, so the call still succeeds
Catches implicit privacy-sensitive data that token-level PII pattern matchers miss, such as a named hospital implying a diagnosis or a timestamp revealing a routine
Is schema-aware and trust-aware, so it redacts differentially: the same field is minimized more aggressively when the destination is an untrusted third party than when it is an internal service
Extends privacy beyond the single response to memory and retrieval, closing leaks that persist long after the turn ends
Assesses leakage against contextual integrity, so it catches disclosure that violates what the user expected even when no single field is individually identifying
Produces a quantitative privacy-cost metric, making the exposure of an agent measurable rather than anecdotal
tradeoffs: Aggressive minimization can strip a field the task actually turns out to need, degrading the result; the rewrite must be validated against task success, not applied blindly
Redaction is lossy and can create brittle downstream behaviour when the tool or the model expected the original field
Schema-aware minimization requires every tool to expose a schema and a declared trust level; an undeclared or undocumented tool silently defeats the mechanism
Implicit-sensitivity classification is itself a judgement call and can produce false positives on placeholder or synthetic data, or miss novel inference-based leaks
Adds a middleware hop on the tool path, costing latency and creating a new component that can fail or be bypassed

Minimization of the prompt sits in tension with utility: models are biased toward oversharing and, empirically, struggle to predict the minimum disclosure a task needs, so the utility-preserving floor is hard to locate
Privacy and task-completeness are genuinely in tension in some agents, and there is no setting of the minimizer that removes that trade-off — only moves it
use_cases: A web-navigation agent that screenshots and acts on pages containing unrelated personal data in the background, minimizing before any screenshot or tool argument leaves the boundary
A support agent whose tool calls would otherwise forward the caller's account, health, or order details to a third-party API that only needs an account identifier
An assistant with persistent memory that minimizes what it stores, so injected or incidentally-seen PII is not retained and re-surfaced in a later session
A tool-using agent whose arguments are rewritten field-by-field to the minimum the receiving tool's schema requires, with privacy cost computed per call
avoid_when: The agent handles no personal or sensitive data, in which case the minimization layer has nothing to act on and only adds latency
Every downstream consumer is fully trusted and internal, where disclosure carries no cross-boundary risk and minimization only costs utility
Data minimisation would defeat the task outright and no lossless narrowing exists, so the choice is privacy or correctness rather than a tunable trade-off
No tool declares a schema or trust level, making schema-aware argument minimization impossible to apply correctly
The task is open-ended research over a corpus the agent must see in full, where the information needed is genuinely the whole input
component_types: redaction filter at the context and memory boundaries
anti_patterns: Relying on system-prompt instructions telling the model not to reveal sensitive data, since prompt-level restrictions are not reliably honoured and are bypassable by injection
Using token-level PII redaction that matches patterns but misses implicit sensitivity, treating 'no PII pattern matched' as 'nothing sensitive is present'
Gating whole calls as allow-or-block when the correct action is to rewrite the arguments to the minimum the schema requires
Applying uniform redaction regardless of the destination's trust level, stripping a field before an internal service while passing it through to an untrusted third party unchanged
Minimizing only the outgoing response while leaving tool-call arguments and persistent memory unfiltered, which is where most real disclosure actually occurs
Persisting raw user input into memory without a minimization or sensitivity scan, so incidental and injected PII is retained indefinitely
Assessing leakage by whether a single field is identifying, ignoring contextual-integrity violations where individually innocuous data jointly exceeds what the user expected to share
design_principles: Minimize proactively at the boundary rather than detect after disclosure, because a rewrite that happens before the call cannot leak
Minimize to the task's actual necessity, preserving task validity, so privacy is achieved by removing the unneeded rather than by blocking the needed
Classify implicit as well as explicit sensitivity, since much real exposure (a diagnosis implied by a facility, a routine implied by a timestamp) is not a PII pattern
Make minimization schema-aware and trust-aware, so what is stripped is governed by what the destination needs and how far it is trusted
Treat memory and retrieval as first-class privacy boundaries, not sinks, because persisted data is disclosed again on every future turn
Evaluate leakage in context against the user's disclosure expectations, because privacy is a property of information flow, not of any single field
Make exposure measurable with a quantitative privacy-cost metric so minimizer changes can be compared rather than argued
best_practices: Deploy a middleware that intercepts tool calls before execution, classifies privacy-sensitive arguments, and rewrites them to the minimum the tool's schema requires
Record a declared schema and trust level for every tool the agent can call, and treat an undeclared tool as untrusted by default
Extend sensitivity beyond named PII to inferred sensitivity (facility names, timestamps, co-occurrence patterns) and measure it in a privacy-cost metric
Scan and minimize before anything is persisted to memory, not only before it is returned, so incidental and injected sensitive data is not retained
Strip placeholder and synthetic PII from enforcement to avoid false positives on test and demo data
Assess information flow against contextual-integrity norms (what the user expected to be shared with this destination) rather than only checking for identifiers
Validate minimization against end-to-end task success so the privacy/utility operating point is explicit and regression-tested, not assumed
